In summary, we don't expect major upgrades from the iPhone 18 Pro over its predecessor. In fact, if you're currently using an older iPhone, there are plenty of reasons to buy an iPhone 17 Pro before next week's new model launch.

Among the few upgrades we anticipate, the biggest one on paper is the variable aperture on the main lens. But in actual use, will this really make a noticeable difference...?

Variable aperture controls depth of field

One of the biggest differences between photos taken with a DSLR or mirrorless camera and those taken with an iPhone is the control over depth of field.

When using a traditional camera, a large aperture can create a shallow depth of field, most commonly used to separate the subject from the background. Portrait photos are the classic example (which is why Apple's simulated shallow depth of field effect is called "Portrait Mode").

Conversely, when shooting landscapes or cityscapes, a small aperture is typically used to ensure everything from the foreground to the background remains sharp and clear.

Therefore, variable aperture has always been a standard feature on any traditional camera lens. In contrast, iPhones have always used fixed-aperture lenses. (There are actually several ways to achieve shallow depth of field on an iPhone, which I'll cover in a separate article after the new model launches, but these are exceptions rather than the norm.)

iPhone lens gains variable aperture

We expect this year's iPhone to be among the first models equipped with a variable aperture lens. It's still unclear whether this feature will be applied to both iPhone 18 Pro models, or limited to the Pro Max only. Either way, it's expected to be limited to the main lens, not the ultra-wide or telephoto lenses.

On paper, this is indeed big news. In theory, a variable aperture lens gives us control over depth of field. But in practice, we shouldn't get too excited about achieving the effect shown in the large image at the top of this article—the reason being that some things won't change.

The bad news

The main limiting factor for iPhones isn't the lens aperture (the aperture itself is already quite large), but the size of the image sensor. All else being equal, the larger the sensor, the more pronounced the shallow depth of field effect can be. Compared to DSLRs and mirrorless cameras, iPhone sensors are much smaller, and that won't change this year.

With the same sensor size and only a slightly larger aperture, according to the laws of physics, we shouldn't expect a huge difference.

The potentially good news

That said, there may still be a glimmer of hope. Adding a mechanical variable aperture to one of the iPhone's lenses is by no means a simple engineering task. Given the compact size of the lens, this design is complex and expensive.

So we need to ask the question: why would Apple put in so much effort and money to do something with rather limited expected benefits? If the final result is only the level of difference predicted by calculations, it's simply not worth doing.

This leads me to speculate—if Apple really plans to make this new feature a major selling point, there must be more behind the scenes.

One possibility I can think of is that this optical upgrade is almost serving as cover for a major improvement to Portrait Mode. The simulated effect has improved year by year, but there's still room for improvement—perhaps relying on the upgraded chip's AI computing power to allow Apple to achieve more natural-looking results?

If that's the case, I reckon most people wouldn't mind this kind of "shortcut"—the variable aperture brings only modest benefits, while the software improvements are actually the key to delivering more significant upgrades. For most people, what matters most is the final result. That's my best guess for now.

Have a better idea? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
